questions.q: What does it mean that a cached value is stale?
questions.explain: A cache holds a copy. When the original changes and the copy does not, the copy is stale. Every caching decision is about how much staleness you can accept in exchange for speed.
options: It was loaded from the database
The real data has changed since the copy was made, so the copy is out of date
It is about to be evicted
It was stored without a TTL

questions.q: Should a shop cache a customer's wallet balance and use the cached value to approve a ₦50,000 purchase?
questions.explain: A stale balance can approve a purchase the customer cannot pay for. You may cache a balance for display, briefly, but the decision itself happens against the real data, usually in one database statement.
options: Yes, as long as the key contains the customer id
No: data used to decide about money or permissions must be read fresh

questions.q: A developer caches carts under the key "cart". What happens?
questions.explain: A key must contain every input that changes the answer. For per-user data that includes the user id. A missing input serves one person's data to another.
options: Nothing bad; the cache is per request
The first customer's cart is served to every customer until the TTL ends: a data leak
Every request misses, so it is only slow
The cache refuses to store objects

questions.q: Why cache "product 999 does not exist" for a few seconds?
questions.explain: This is negative caching. Without it, a script requesting random ids bypasses the cache completely. Keep the TTL short, because "does not exist yet" is exactly what may change soon.
options: So a flood of requests for ids that do not exist does not reach the database every time
Because missing products are never created later
So the 404 page loads faster in the browser

questions.q: On a price change, in which order should the code touch the database and the cache?
questions.explain: If you delete first, a reader can miss in between, load the old price and cache it again. Updating first and deleting after closes that gap (a small race remains, which generations handle).
options: Delete the cache key, then update the database
Update the database, then delete the cache key
Update the cache with the new price, then the database

questions.q: Why does the lesson invalidate by deleting the key instead of writing the new value into the cache?
questions.explain: Writing values from the write path duplicates the loading logic (joins, mapping, formatting), and any difference produces wrong cache entries. A delete always leads to a correct reload.
options: Deleting is the only operation Redis supports
The next read reloads through the one normal loading path, so the cached value is always built the same way
Writing to a cache is slower than deleting
Updating the cache would change the TTL

questions.q: Which two jobs does a TTL do in a cache-aside setup?
questions.explain: Even with careful invalidation, some write path will one day forget to delete a key. The TTL guarantees the wrong copy disappears eventually.
options: It encrypts the value and sets its size
It bounds how stale a value can get, and it cleans up after invalidations you forgot
It decides the cache key and the eviction order

questions.q: Why does TtlCache take a Clock instead of calling Date.now()?
questions.explain: With a manual clock, "60 seconds later" is one line in a test, and the result is the same on every run. Waiting for real time makes tests slow and flaky.
options: So tests can move time forward instantly and check exact TTL boundaries
So the cache can run in the browser

questions.q: In TtlCache.get, a hit deletes the key and sets it again. Why?
questions.explain: Re-inserting marks the entry as most recently used. When the cache is full, entries.keys().next().value is then the least recently used key. The expiry time is kept unchanged.
options: A Map keeps insertion order, so moving the key to the end keeps the least recently used key first, ready to be evicted
To copy the value so callers cannot change it
It is a bug; it makes every hit a miss

questions.q: What happens to an in-process cache with no size limit on a busy server?
questions.explain: Expired entries in this cache are only removed when read, and even with sweeping, many unique keys can be alive at once. A size limit with LRU eviction makes memory use predictable.
options: It grows with every new key until the process runs out of memory
The TTL keeps it small without further help

questions.q: A warm-up job caches 10,000 products at once with a TTL of exactly 60 seconds. What problem does jitter solve?
questions.explain: Random spread (for example ±10%) turns one synchronized expiry into a steady trickle of reloads.
options: Values being served in the wrong order
All 10,000 entries expiring in the same moment and missing together, which spikes the database

questions.q: A reader starts loading, a writer updates the price and deletes the key, then the reader stores the old price. Which fix does the lesson use?
questions.explain: The generation tells a loader that the world changed while it was working. Its result may still be returned to its own caller, but it is not stored for everyone else.
options: Deleting the key before updating the database
A generation per key: invalidation increases it, and a loader only stores its result if the generation has not changed

questions.q: What is a cache stampede?
questions.explain: It happens exactly when a hot key is empty or has just expired, which is when the database most needs the cache's protection.
options: A cache that stores too many keys
Many requests missing the same key at the same moment and all loading it from the database
Two servers writing the same key

questions.q: Each of ten servers uses in-process single-flight. A hot key expires in the shared cache. At most how many database reads for that key follow?
questions.explain: Single-flight collapses concurrent loads inside one process. Across processes, you need a shared lock (such as Redis SET … NX PX) if even ten reads are too many.
options: 0, because single-flight serves the stale value

questions.q: Why must a distributed cache lock such as SET lock:product:1 <id> NX PX 5000 have an expiry?
questions.explain: NX sets the key only if it is absent (so one server wins); PX 5000 makes it disappear after 5 seconds no matter what happens to its owner.
options: Redis requires every key to have one
If the server holding the lock crashes, the lock would otherwise never be released and nobody could reload the key
So other servers can read the value while it is locked

questions.q: An entry is past its fresh time but still inside its stale window. What does a stale-while-revalidate cache do?
questions.explain: Nobody waits unless the entry is completely too old. The next request after the refresh gets the new value. HTTP has the same idea: Cache-Control: stale-while-revalidate.
options: Waits for the database, then returns the new value
Returns the stale value immediately and starts one background refresh
Returns an error until the refresh finishes

questions.q: After a deploy, the cache's hit rate falls from 92% to 3%, and nothing else changed in the traffic. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: A key that contains something unique per request (a timestamp, a request id, an unnormalised query string) never repeats, so every lookup misses. Watching the hit rate is how you notice.
options: The keys changed shape, for example a new value in the key that is different for almost every request

questions.q: The shared cache is down. What should a product page do?
questions.explain: For data that also lives in the database, the cache is an optimisation. Losing it must cost speed, not correctness or availability. Make sure the database can take the extra load for a while.
options: Show an error page until the cache is back
Fail open: count the error and read from the database, so the site is slower but still works

questions.q: Why should every call to a shared cache have a short timeout?
questions.explain: "Down" fails fast; "slow" holds every request hostage. A timeout turns slow into down, which fail-open code already handles.
options: Because caches return stale data after a timeout
A cache that hangs makes every request wait; a fast failure lets the request fall back to the database

questions.q: A search page caches results under search:${rawQueryString}. What is the risk?
questions.explain: Unbounded keys from raw input let an attacker, or just random tracking parameters, churn the cache. Normalise inputs (sort, drop unknown parameters, lower-case) and cache only known shapes.
options: Anyone can send endless different query strings, filling the cache with junk and evicting useful entries
Nothing: more keys means a better hit rate

questions.q: Four servers each keep an in-memory cache of prices. An admin changes a price through server 1, which deletes its own entry. What do customers on servers 2 to 4 see?
questions.explain: Each process only invalidates its own memory. Use a shared cache, broadcast invalidations (for example Redis pub/sub), or accept the TTL as the staleness bound.
options: The old price until each server's entry expires

questions.q: Why must a cache not store the result of a failed load?
questions.explain: A brief database hiccup would become a minute-long outage for that key. Store only successful values; the next caller retries the load.
options: The failure would be served to everyone for the whole TTL, even after the database has recovered
It would count as a hit
Errors are always too large to cache

questions.q: A cache with room for two entries evicts the least recently used one. What does this print?
questions.explain: Reading rice moved it to the end, so oil became the least recently used entry and was evicted when sugar arrived.

questions.q: An entry is stored at time 1,000 with a TTL of 500 ms, and it counts as expired when expiresAt <= now. What does this print?
questions.explain: The entry lives for exactly 500 ms: alive at 1,499, gone at 1,500. Tests with a manual clock check exactly this boundary.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each of the four distinct products misses once (p1, p2, p3, p4); the repeats of p1 (three) and p2 (one) are hits. The hit rate is 4 of 8.

questions.q: The cache uses undefined to mean "not cached". What does this print?
questions.explain: The value undefined is stored, but a later lookup cannot tell it from "not cached", so every request loads again. Cache "not found" as null (or wrap values) so negative caching works.

questions.q: Some products are free samples with price 0. What does this print?
questions.explain: if (cached) treats the cached 0 as a miss, so the free sample is read from the database every time (4 reads) while rice is read once. Check cached !== undefined instead.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The three concurrent calls share one load. After it settles, finally removes the entry, so a later call starts a new load. Single-flight collapses concurrent work; it is not a cache by itself.

questions.q: Prices are shown in naira or dollars, but the key forgets the currency. What does this print?
questions.explain: The currency changes the answer but is not in the key, so the first request's answer is served to the second. The key must be price:1:NGN and price:1:USD.

questions.q: An entry is fresh for 60 s and usable while stale for another 300 s. It was stored at t = 0. What does this print?
questions.explain: The stale window starts at 60 s and ends at 60 + 300 = 360 s. Only after that does a request have to wait for the database. (Node prints the array on several lines because it is long.)
options: [ 'fresh', 'fresh', 'stale: serve and refresh', 'stale: serve and refresh' ]

[
  'fresh',
  'stale: serve and refresh',
  'stale: serve and refresh',
  'expired: load and wait'
]
[ 'fresh', 'stale: serve and refresh', 'expired: load and wait', 'expired: load and wait' ]

questions.q: A value goes into a shared cache as JSON and comes back. What does this print?
questions.explain: A Date becomes an ISO string and a Map becomes an empty object. Values in a shared cache need a deliberate format, like a DTO, and conversion back when read.

questions.q: Five requests miss the same key at once and use plain cache-aside. What does this print?
questions.explain: All five checked the cache before any of them had stored the value, so all five went to the database. The sixth request, after they finished, was a hit. That is a stampede in miniature.

questions.q: A loader remembers the generation it started with. What does this print?
questions.explain: The slow reader started at generation 0, but an invalidation moved the key to generation 1, so its old price is not stored. A reader that starts after the invalidation stores the new price.

questions.q: Finish get: return the value if expiresAt is still in the future, otherwise delete the entry and return undefined. The clock is a plain variable here.
questions.explain: Checking the expiry on read (lazy expiry) is enough to never serve an old value; deleting the entry at the same time frees its memory.

questions.q: Finish set so the cache never holds more than MAX entries: after inserting, evict the least recently used key (the first key of the Map) and count the eviction.
questions.explain: Deleting before setting moves an existing key to the end. The first key of the Map is the oldest, so it is the one to evict. Counting evictions shows whether the cache is too small.

questions.q: Write cacheAside(key, load): return the cached value on a hit (count it), otherwise load, store and return it (count a miss).
questions.explain: The first call misses and fills the cache; the next three are hits. The counters are the raw material for the hit rate.

questions.q: Write run(key, work) so concurrent calls for the same key share one running promise, which is removed when it settles.
questions.explain: Twenty callers, one load. finally cleans up after success and after failure, so a failed load is not remembered.

questions.q: Write cacheKey(page, customerId, currency) that includes every input and a version, in the form shop:v2:PAGE:CUSTOMER:CURRENCY.
questions.explain: Every input that changes the answer is in the key, so two customers never share an entry. The version lets a new release ignore entries in an old format.

questions.q: Finish ttlFor(product): 60 seconds for a found product, 5 seconds for null (not found).
questions.explain: Negative entries protect the database from floods of missing ids, but a product that does not exist yet may be created any moment, so its entry should expire soon.

questions.q: Write getProduct so that a failing cache is counted in cacheErrors and the product is still loaded from the database.
questions.explain: Fail open: the cache error is recorded for monitoring, and the request continues to the source of truth. The customer sees a slower page, not an error page.
questions.expected:
product 1 from the database
cache errors: 1

questions.q: Write hitRate(stats) that returns the hit rate as a percentage with one decimal, like "75.0%", and "n/a" when there were no lookups.
questions.explain: Hits divided by all lookups. Guarding against zero lookups avoids printing NaN% on a freshly started server.
